answer_text:
Switching the US to the metric system would be an **enormously complex and costly undertaking** — arguably the largest measurement transition in human history. Here's a comprehensive breakdown of why:

---

## 🏛️ Legal & Political Background

U.S. customary units have been defined in terms of metric units since the 19th century, and according to U.S. law, the metric system has been the "preferred system of weights and measures for United States trade and commerce" since 1975. The U.S. even has a national policy to adopt the metric system. However, under Executive Order 12770, signed in 1991 by President George H.W. Bush, all U.S. agencies were required to adopt the metric system — but conversion was made non-mandatory, so U.S. customary units remain in common use in government and many industries.

In 1866, Congress authorized the use of the metric system and officially recognized it, but did not mandate its use. There was no strong push or compelling reason to switch fully to metric. Further, in 1975, the Metric Conversion Act promoted metrication, but again it was not mandatory — it left adoption up to individual industries, and without legal compulsion, few sectors saw the benefit of making the switch.

---

## 💰 The Financial Cost

The biggest reasons the U.S. hasn't adopted the metric system are simply time and money.

The U.S. retains the imperial system primarily due to the immense economic costs of converting industrial, manufacturing, and transportation infrastructure. Additionally, deep-rooted familiarity, a lack of mandatory federal adoption, and the logistical challenge of replacing billions of dollars' worth of equipment make the transition impractical.

For a sense of scale, we only have to look to Canada to get a sense of what switching would take. Canada went metric back in 1970, and it took about 15 years and more than $1 billion to update everything. The U.S. is many times larger and more complex.

In 2015, NASA estimated a total conversion to the metric system would cost them $370 million alone — but sixteen years earlier, they lost $125 million when the Mars Climate Orbiter crashed due to confusion over units.

---

## 🔧 Infrastructure Challenges

The scope of physical changes required is staggering:

- **Road signs:** Every speed limit sign would have to be changed from miles per hour to kilometers per hour — and so would every sign on every city street, country road, and freeway across the nation.
- **Manufacturing:** When the Industrial Revolution began, the machinery used in factories was developed to size in imperial units, all workers were trained to deal with imperial units, and many products were made to feature imperial units. Overhauling all of that today would be a massive undertaking.
- **Industry:** When the rest of the world switched to metric, it was mostly before or at the very beginning of the industrial revolution. Today, with mass production of goods, switching everything over to a new measurement system would be a gigantic undertaking — by far the largest, most complex transition of measurement systems in human history.

---

## 📚 Education

The education system is perhaps the hardest hit. Both U.S. customary and metric are taught, but students required to learn two measurement systems will more likely be confused, and the extra time spent teaching both systems has its own implied cost. They are disadvantaged against students in other countries who only need to know one system. One researcher estimated that a conversion to a single measurement system would save roughly 71 days in the classroom, and a full conversion to metric would save over $17 billion.

---

## 🧠 Cultural Resistance

The simple answer for why America hasn't gone full-on metric is that the overwhelming majority of Americans have never wanted to.

Whenever the discussion of switching unit systems arose in Congress, the passage of a bill favoring the metric system was thwarted by big businesses and American citizens who didn't want to go through the time-consuming and expensive hassle. Many also believed the U.S. should keep its particular system, setting it apart from other countries.

According to a 2016 poll, only 32% of Americans want to convert.

---

## ✅ The U.S. Is Already Partially Metric

Interestingly, American manufacturers have put out all-metric cars, and the wine and spirits industry abandoned fifths for 750-milliliter bottles. The metric system is, quietly and behind the scenes, now the standard in most industries, with a few notable exceptions like construction.

Many U.S. industries heavily use the metric system, especially those with international ties or reliant on modern technology, including science, medicine, automotive, electronics, and manufacturing. Examples include pharmaceutical dosages in milligrams, automotive parts in millimeters, and aviation using Celsius for temperature.

---

## 🔑 Bottom Line

Switching to the metric system in the U.S. would be **extremely difficult** — not because it's technically impossible, but because of the sheer scale of infrastructure changes, enormous short-term costs, deep cultural resistance, and the lack of any political will to make it mandatory. Replacing a measurement system with another requires significant investment, though organizations that have converted generally found that costs were less than anticipated and that the efficiency benefits exceeded the cost of conversion in the long run. The challenge is convincing a nation of 330+ million people — and its industries — to take that leap.
